title: Eye Irritation - Chalazion
patient_instructions: You are Jimmy, a 40-year-old office worker who has come to your GP because of irritation in one eye. Open with: 'Doctor, I've had this irritation in my eye that's been bothering me.' If the candidate clarifies what you mean, reveal that there is a small lump on your left lower eyelid. Describe it as a firm lump on the lower lid, present for about three weeks, slowly appeared, and it is only mildly tender/uncomfortable rather than very painful (if pushed, say it does not really hurt much). No redness spreading, no discharge, no itch. Your vision is normal, no double vision, no light sensitivity, no flashes/floaters, no pain on moving the eye. No fever, headache, nausea, runny nose, tiredness or rash. You do not wear contact lenses, no trauma, no eye cosmetics, no contact with unwell people. This is your first time with this. No past eye problems and no family history of skin cancer. Your idea: 'I thought it might be a stye.' Your concern: 'will it need surgery?' and 'is it something serious?' Your expectation: to know what it is and how to treat it. Affect: calm, mildly annoyed by the irritation. When the candidate is given the photograph, it shows a discrete lump on the lateral lower lid.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP in a face-to-face consultation. Jimmy, 40, presents with irritation in one eye. Take a focused history, then after a prompt the examiner will hand you a clinical photograph. Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient, and outline your management. Assume a physical examination card is available on request; there is no separate examination task.
examiner_instructions: The diagnosis is a chalazion (blocked meibomian gland) - a firm, characteristically PAINLESS chronic granuloma. Do not reward a candidate who simply calls any tender lid lump a chalazion; strong candidates distinguish a tender lump (stye/hordeolum or infected chalazion) from the classically non-tender chalazion. First-line management is conservative per RACGP: warm compresses 10-15 minutes 3-4 times daily, gentle lid massage toward the lashes, and lid hygiene; refer for intralesional steroid or incision and curettage if not resolving at 4-6 weeks. Reward candidates who note antibiotics are NOT routinely needed. Critically, the must-not-miss red flag is a RECURRENT chalazion at the same site, lash loss (madarosis) or an ulcerated/indurated lesion in an older patient - refer to exclude sebaceous (meibomian) gland carcinoma or BCC. Provide photograph on request (discrete lateral lower-lid lump) and the examination card (visual acuity, movements, pupils, temperature all normal) if asked.

criteria: Clarifies 'irritation' (pain vs gritty sensation vs lump) and characterises the lump (site, tenderness, surface, duration, recurrence, enlarging)
Systematic eyelid and eye screen (swelling, discharge, vision, photophobia, flashes/floaters, pain on eye movement)
Screens systemic and infective features (fever, headache, sinus symptoms) and risk factors (contact lenses, trauma, cosmetics)
Records/asks for visual acuity even for a simple lid lump
Correctly identifies chalazion as a blocked meibomian gland and recognises it is characteristically firm and painless
Distinguishes chalazion (deep, meibomian, tarsal plate) from stye/hordeolum (lid margin, glands of Zeis/Moll, tender)
Offers relevant differentials including blepharitis and, for a persistent/recurrent lump, eyelid malignancy (sebaceous carcinoma, BCC)
First-line conservative management: warm compresses 10-15 min 3-4x/day, lid massage toward lashes, lid hygiene (RACGP)
States antibiotics not routinely required; referral for intralesional steroid or incision and curettage if unresolved at 4-6 weeks
Recognises red flag: recurrent same-site chalazion, lash loss or ulceration warrants referral for lid biopsy to exclude malignancy
Explains the condition and self-care in plain, reassuring language and checks understanding
Addresses patient's concern about surgery/seriousness and provides safety-netting for non-resolution

red_flags: Recurrent chalazion at the same site, especially unilateral with loss of eyelashes (madarosis) in an older patient - exclude sebaceous (meibomian) gland carcinoma
Ulcerated, indurated or bleeding eyelid lesion - refer to exclude basal cell carcinoma (Murtagh: refer patients with eyelid ulcers)
A painless, progressively enlarging lump should raise suspicion of tumour
Any reduction in vision, marked pain, photophobia or spreading periorbital swelling (suggesting preseptal/orbital cellulitis) rather than a simple lid lump
australian_guidelines: RACGP / Murtagh Patient Education - chalazion (meibomian cyst): first-line warm compresses, lid massage and lid hygiene; refer for intralesional steroid or incision and curettage if unresolved at 4-6 weeks
Murtagh red-eye golden rules - always test and record vision, and refer patients with eyelid ulcers

Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - antibiotics are not routinely indicated for uncomplicated chalazion; reserve for associated bacterial conjunctivitis/blepharitis (and systemic antibiotics for preseptal cellulitis)
eTG / RACGP - chronic meibomian gland dysfunction/blepharitis may be managed with lid hygiene +/- oral doxycycline
learning_objectives: Differentiate a chalazion from a stye/hordeolum on the basis of gland involved, depth and tenderness
Deliver first-line conservative management for a chalazion per RACGP
Recognise the red flags for eyelid malignancy masquerading as a recurrent chalazion
Apply the red-eye golden rules including recording visual acuity for any lid lesion
key_points: A chalazion is a firm, PAINLESS chronic granuloma of a meibomian gland; a tender lump favours a stye or infected chalazion.
A recurrent, same-site chalazion with lash loss in an older patient is sebaceous gland carcinoma until proven otherwise - refer for full-thickness lid biopsy.
Antibiotics are not routinely needed for an uncomplicated chalazion.
Always test and record visual acuity, even for a simple eyelid lump.

citations.claim: Infective conjunctivitis produces a gritty/sandy sensation with discharge and is usually bilateral; clarifying 'irritation' helps separate lid pathology from conjunctivitis.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.486

citations.claim: Red-eye golden rules - always test and record vision and refer patients with eyelid ulcers; Murtagh provides patient-education handouts on chalazion (meibomian cyst) and blepharitis used for management.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1207

citations.claim: A painless, progressive swelling should raise suspicion of tumour and prompt urgent referral - the red-flag principle applied to a recurrent eyelid lump (possible sebaceous carcinoma).
citations.source: Churchills Pocketbook of Differential Diagnosis, p.249
